table.title: Do long-term meditators stress less? Affective and autonomic responses to acute stress
table.statistical_tests:
All analyses will be conducted in R (version ≥ 4.3) using lm() and lme4::lmer() for frequentist models, BIC-approximation Bayes Factors for the autonomic model comparison, and a custom bootstrap implementation for mediation. Two-tailed alpha = .05 throughout. Continuous moderators are grand-mean-centred prior to entry. Group is coded 0 = control, 1 = meditator. Female is coded 1 = female, 0 = otherwise.
Model H1a — Post-stress negative affect (primary). Linear regression (ANCOVA framework):
PANAS_Post_Neg ~ Group + PANAS_Pre_Neg + Age + Female
The Group coefficient is the primary test. Effect size: partial η² for Group (Type III sums of squares).Model H1b — Post-stress positive affect (primary). Linear regression:
PANAS_Post_Pos ~ Group + PANAS_Pre_Pos + Age + Female
The Group coefficient is the primary test.

Model H2 — Bayesian model comparison (primary). Three nested linear mixed-effects models are fit to the long-format HRV data (one row per participant per phase):
Full: lnRMSSD ~ Group * Phase + Age + Female + (1 | Participant)
No interaction: lnRMSSD ~ Group + Phase + Age + Female + (1 | Participant)
No group: lnRMSSD ~ Phase + Age + Female + (1 | Participant)
Phase is a 3-level within-subject factor (baseline, anticipation, recovery), with baseline as the reference level. All three models are fitted by maximum likelihood (REML = FALSE).Bayes Factors are computed via BIC approximation (Wagenmakers, 2007): BF10 = exp((BIC_reduced − BIC_full) / 2). Two BFs are reported:
BF for Group × Phase interaction = comparison of full vs. no-interaction models
BF for Group main effect = comparison of no-interaction vs. no-group models
Frequentist robustness for H2. The same three nested models are compared by likelihood ratio tests (LR χ²) and reported alongside the Bayes Factors. The full LMM fixed-effect estimates are reported with 95% CIs.
Manipulation check for HRV. A reduced model lnRMSSD ~ Phase + Age + Female + (1 | Participant) is fit to verify that the expected within-subject pattern emerges (baseline > anticipation, with partial recovery). 

Model H3 — Emotion regulation as a mediator of group differences in affect (exploratory). 
For each affect subscale (Negative, Positive), affect is modelled in long format with Time coded 0 = pre, 1 = post; DERS_Total is grand-mean-centred.
a-path: DERS_Total ~ Group + Age + Female
b/c′ model: Affect ~ Group*Time + DERS_Total + DERS_Total:Time + Age + Female + (1 | Participant)
Two indirect effects share the a-path: on baseline affect = a × b₍level₎ (DERS_Total coefficient), and on the stress response = a × b₍change₎ (DERS_Total:Time coefficient). The dissociation is tested as their difference, a × (b₍level₎ − b₍change₎); we tentatively expect an effect on baseline but not on the stress response.
table.transformations:
Phase (HRV models) is a three-level within-subject factor coded with treatment contrasts: baseline (reference), anticipation, recovery.


lnRMSSD. RMSSD values per phase are natural-log-transformed to address positive skew prior to all analyses involving heart-rate variability. Both raw RMSSD and lnRMSSD are retained in the dataset; all inferential analyses use lnRMSSD.

Continuous moderators in interaction models are grand-mean-centred (variable minus sample mean) prior to entry. 

lnRMSSD reactivity and recovery indices are computed as described in the Indices section: lnRMSSD_reactivity = lnRMSSD_anticipation − lnRMSSD_baseline; lnRMSSD_recovery = lnRMSSD_recovery_phase − lnRMSSD_anticipation. Both are on the log scale.
table.inference_criteria:
All frequentist tests use two-tailed alpha = .05. P-values are not adjusted for multiple comparisons within the primary hypothesis set, as each tests a conceptually distinct construct (negative affect, positive affect).
For ANCOVA models (H1), the primary statistic is the Group coefficient and its p-value, with partial η² as effect size (Type III SS). 
For mediation (H3), the inferential criterion is the 95% percentile bootstrap CIs (5,000 resamples, resampling whole participants). An effect or the dissociation is supported when its CI excludes zero. No familywise correction (exploratory).
For the autonomic outcome (H2), inference uses Bayesian model comparison via BIC approximation (Wagenmakers, 2007): BF₁₀ = exp((BIC_reduced − BIC_full) / 2). Two BFs are reported: Group × Phase interaction (full vs. no-interaction) and Group main effect (no-interaction vs. no-group). The HRV manipulation check is confirmed when the omnibus Phase effect is significant (p < .05) with the baseline-to-anticipation contrast negative.
Bayes Factor thresholds (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013): >100 extreme, >30 very strong, >10 strong, >3 moderate, 1–3 anecdotal. BF < 1 indicates evidence for the alternative model (e.g., BF₀₁ > 3 = moderate evidence for the null).
table.research_questions: The project addresses three questions in long-term meditators relative to meditation-naïve controls: (1) whether they show attenuated affective responses to acute social-evaluative stress; (2) whether they differ in cardiac vagal responses across baseline, anticipation, and recovery phases of the TSST; and (3) whether trait emotion regulation difficulties statistically mediate group differences in responses to acute stress.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data exists but the authors have not observed it yet. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists and is possible for the authors to access. However, the authors certify that they have not accessed any of that data and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.study_design_overview: The dataset comprises 149 community-dwelling adults aged 19–68 years: 81 long-term mindfulness meditators with a minimum of three years of consistent practice (at least three sessions per week, at least 15 minutes per session), and 68 meditation-naïve controls matched on age, gender, and education. All participants completed the Trier Social Stress Test (Kirschbaum et al., 1993). Self-reported affect (PANAS) was measured before and after the stressor. Cardiac vagal tone (lnRMSSD from electrocardiography) was assessed in a subsample of 70 participants across baseline, anticipation, and post-stress recovery phases. Emotion regulation difficulties (DERS), and meditation practice variables (lifetime months of practice; recent practice minutes per month) were also assessed.
table.data_collection_procedures:
This is a secondary analysis of existing data collected as part of a broader research programme at the Department of Psychology, University of Amsterdam, which also included functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data acquisition. 

Meditators were recruited through the meditation centres and local mindfulness communities in the Netherlands. Controls were recruited via flyers and online advertisements. Participants received 30 € as compensation.

Eligibility criteria for meditators included: age between 18 and 68 years, a minimum of three years of consistent mindfulness practice, with at least 15 minutes of practice three times per week (equivalent to a minimum of 7020 minutes of lifetime practice). Control participants had no history of consistent mindfulness practice. Groups were matched on age and gender.

Exclusion criteria included: pregnancy, claustrophobia, metal or electronic implants (e.g., pacemakers, aneurysm clips), history of head trauma, fainting, neurological disorders (e.g., strokes, tumors), recent treatment for psychological disorders or substance abuse (past 12 months), use of substances known to affect brain function (e.g., painkillers, sleeping aids), heavy alcohol use (more than 10 drinks per week), or heavy smoking (more than 140 cigarettes per week).

table.manipulated_variables: This study has no randomization. Group membership (long-term meditator vs. meditation-naïve control) is a quasi-experimental between-subjects classification based on participants' pre-existing meditation history, not an experimental manipulation. The Trier Social Stress Test was administered identically to all participants and is therefore a within-subjects procedural event rather than a manipulated factor.
table.measured_variables:
Outcome variables
1. Self-reported affect (PANAS). The Positive and Negative Affect Schedule – Short Form (Thompson, 2007) was administered immediately before and after the TSST. Ten items rated on a 5-point Likert scale yield two 5-item subscales: Positive Affect and Negative Affect (each scored 5–25). 

2. Cardiac vagal tone (lnRMSSD). Root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) of inter-beat intervals, derived from continuous ECG (Polar H10) and processed in Kubios HRV Scientific 4.2.0 with the Lipponen and Tarvainen (2019) artefact-correction algorithm and smoothness-priors detrending (λ = 500). RMSSD will be extracted for three TSST phases — baseline (5 min rest), anticipation (two 2-min pre-speech periods averaged), and recovery (5 min rest), and natural-log-transformed. Phases with greater than 5% corrected beats or less than 3.5 min of valid recording will be excluded. 

Main predictors 
Group. Binary between-subjects classification: long-term mindfulness meditator (1) vs. meditation-naïve control (0).

Mediator and exploratory predictors
DERS Total (Gratz & Roemer, 2004). 36-item self-report measure of trait emotion regulation difficulties; total score (range 36–180) is the primary mediator.

Meditation practice (meditator subsample). MonthsPractice (total months of consistent practice; square-root-transformed) and MinsLastMonth (minutes practised in the month before the session; natural-log-transformed).
table.indices:
PANAS subscale scores. Each PANAS subscale (Positive Affect, Negative Affect) is the unweighted sum of its five constituent items at each timepoint.

lnRMSSD per phase. For each TSST phase (baseline, anticipation, recovery), lnRMSSD = ln(RMSSD), where RMSSD is the root mean square of successive differences of inter-beat intervals computed by Kubios HRV Scientific 4.2.0 over the relevant phase window. The anticipation value is the arithmetic mean of lnRMSSD computed from the two 2-minute pre-speech preparation windows (lnRMSSD_S1a and lnRMSSD_S1b averaged).

lnRMSSD reactivity and recovery indices. Two within-subject difference scores on the log scale:
lnRMSSD_reactivity = lnRMSSD_anticipation − lnRMSSD_baseline
lnRMSSD_recovery = lnRMSSD_recovery_phase − lnRMSSD_anticipation
Negative reactivity values indicate vagal withdrawal under anticipation; positive recovery values indicate vagal rebound after the stressor.

DERS Total. Unweighted sum of all 36 DERS items (range 36–180), with reverse-keyed items recoded prior to summation per Gratz and Roemer (2004).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Inclusion criteria (participant level): All participants who completed the laboratory protocol and provided at least the primary affective outcome data (pre-stress and post-stress PANAS) are included in the analytic sample (N = 149). No further exclusions are applied at the participant level for the affective analyses.

Exclusion criteria (observation level, HRV only). Heart-rate variability data are subject to two phase-level quality criteria, applied independently to each TSST phase per participant:

Artefact correction threshold. A phase is excluded if the Kubios artefact-correction algorithm (Lipponen & Tarvainen, 2019) flagged more than 5% of beats for correction.
Recording duration threshold. A phase is excluded if less than 3.5 minutes of valid recording remain after artefact rejection.

text.text: • We tested affective and autonomic stressor responses in long-term meditators.
• Meditators reported lower negative and higher positive affect after the stressor.
• Meditators and controls showed comparable autonomic responses to the stressor.
• Emotion regulation accounted for baseline affect differences, not affective change.
• Meditators reported fewer and less severe stressors over the preceding year.

Mindfulness meditation and similar contemplative practices have been associated with improved mental and physical health (Black & Slavich, 2016; Creswell et al., 2019; Galante et al., 2023; Goldberg et al., 2018), but why these benefits occur remains unclear.
text.formatted: Mindfulness meditation and similar contemplative practices have been associated with improved mental and physical health <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Black & Slavich, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Creswell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Galante et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Goldberg et al., 2018)</ref>, but why these benefits occur remains unclear.

text.text: One influential theoretical account is that mindfulness changes how people respond to stress.

Building on the original stress-buffering hypothesis (Cohen & Wills, 1985), Creswell and colleagues (2014; 2019) proposed that mindfulness alters stress appraisals so that stressors are perceived as less threatening, with corresponding reduction in both affective and physiological stress responses.

text.text: These attenuated responses are, in turn, thought to explain the downstream effects of mindfulness on health.

Because repeated and prolonged activation of the stress response systems contributes to the onset and exacerbation of stress-related disease (Evans et al., 2025; Juster et al., 2010; McEwen, 2008; McEwen & Stellar, 1993; Parker et al., 2022; Shields & Slavich, 2017), reduced stress reactivity is indeed a plausible mechanism through which mindfulness could be beneficial.

text.text: Although the mindfulness stress-buffering account was developed primarily in the context of trait mindfulness and standardised, typically eight-week mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), these effects should also be observable in long-term meditators.
In particular, years of sustained practice may cultivate greater acceptance-based emotion regulation capacities, which are associated with reduced affective reactivity (Raugh et al., 2025).

text.text: The biological basis of the mindfulness stress-buffering account includes complementary topdown and bottom-up pathways (Creswell & Lindsay, 2014).

text.text: In the brain, mindfulness is thought to strengthen recruitment of prefrontal regulatory regions and reduce reactivity in stress-related regions such as the amygdala (Way et al., 2010).

text.text: It can therefore be used to test the extent to which long-term mindfulness meditation is associated with altered autonomic stress responding, whereas self-reported affect provides a measure of affective response to stress that the stress-buffering account also predicts.

Despite these possibilities, empirical support for autonomic and affective stress-buffering comes almost entirely from MBIs (typically eight weeks of training in previously inexperienced participants) rather than long-term practice.
For example, a meta-analysis of 19 randomised controlled trials found that MBIs do not increase HRV during rest (Brown et al., 2021).

text.text: When looking specifically at HRV in response to stress, the evidence is less conclusive.

For example, a recent scoping review found more adaptive HRV reactivity following MBIs, but this effect was apparent only in more rigorously designed studies of non-clinical populations (Christodoulou et al., 2020).

text.text: Long-term meditators, who accumulate years of regular practice, therefore offer a stronger test of whether sustained practice is associated with altered affective and autonomic responses to acute stress.

Direct tests in long-term meditators are necessarily cross-sectional and remain scarce, in part due to the difficulty of recruiting this rare population into in-person laboratory stress paradigms, such as the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993).

A recent review synthesised the autonomic correlates of long-term meditation across sixteen studies that did not use laboratory stress paradigms (Sezer & Sacchet, 2025).

It thus remains inconclusive whether the differences implied by the stress-buffering account extend to autonomic and affective responses in long-term mindfulness meditators.
That experienced meditators "stress less" is therefore among the most widely assumed claims about contemplative practice, but among the least directly tested.
Less often considered is whether attenuated physiological reactivity would indicate better regulation at all.

Vagal withdrawal during acute challenge is the normative mobilising response, and a growing literature indicates that blunted physiological responses to acute stress are associated with adverse rather than favourable outcomes, including depression, obesity, addiction, and impaired motivated behaviour (Carroll et al., 2017; Lovallo, 2011).

text.text: From this perspective, an adaptive response to acute stress is not damped responding, but appropriate mobilisation followed by efficient recovery.
Whether long-term practice should reduce stress reactivity, preserve it, or alter only parts of it needs to be investigated further.
To address this critical gap, we compared long-term meditators with meditation-naïve, matched controls on affective and autonomic responses to an acute psychosocial stressor (i.e., the TSST).
Our primary aim was to test whether meditators differ from controls in their affective and autonomic responses to the acute psychosocial stressor.

Following the mindfulness stressbuffering account (Creswell & Lindsay, 2014; Creswell et al., 2019), we hypothesised that, relative to controls, meditators would report lower negative affect and higher positive affect following the stressor, after accounting for pre-stress affect.

text.text: In addition to testing whether affective and autonomic differences exist, we explored processes that might explain such differences.

First, because differences in stressor exposure could provide an alternative explanation for any group difference in stress responses, we compared meditators and controls on lifetime stressor exposure.

Second, the stress-buffering account attributes the benefits of sustained practice partly to greater acceptance-based emotion regulation (Lindsay & Creswell, 2017; Raugh et al., 2025), and difficulties in emotion regulation are themselves linked to both affective and autonomic functioning (Williams et al., 2015).

text.text: We thus tested whether group differences in affect were statistically mediated by trait emotion-regulation difficulties, hypothesising that lower emotion-regulation difficulties in meditators would account for group differences in affective responding.
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Method</head>

text.text: This was a cross-sectional study combining a naturalistic lifetime stressor exposure assessment with a laboratory-based experimental stressor paradigm in which we compared long-term mindfulness meditators with meditation-naive controls on affective and autonomic responses to the acute psychosocial stressor.
Data were collected as a part of a larger research project that also included functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), but the present report concerns the acute-stress protocol only.
All participants were tested in a single laboratory session at the University of Amsterdam between June 2022 and February 2026.

The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences, University of Amsterdam (project number 2022-CP-14705), and all participants provided written informed consent.
Both groups were recruited through the participant recruitment platform of the University of Amsterdam, flyers, social media, and snowball sampling.
Long-term meditators were additionally recruited through direct contact with meditation centres across the Netherlands.
Participants received €30 as compensation.
The two groups were matched on age and gender at the group level, by recruiting controls to approximate the age and gender distribution of the meditator sample.
The final sample consisted of 148 adults aged 19-68 years, with 80 long-term mindfulness meditators and 68 control participants.
Autonomic (HRV) data were available for a subsample of 70 participants (37 meditators, 33 controls).
Further details on the demographic characteristics of the sample can be found in Table 1.

text.text: The inclusion criteria for the meditator group were at least three years of consistent mindfulness meditation practice with a minimum weekly practice of three 15-minute sessions.
This corresponded to a minimum of 7020 minutes of lifetime practice.
On average, meditators in our sample far exceeded this threshold, with a mean of 8.4 years of practice (M = 100.8 months, Mdn = 72 months, range = 3-30 years).

37.5% of meditators practiced primarily traditional forms (e.g., Zen, Vipassana), 25.0% primarily secular forms (e.g., Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction), and 37.5% reported regularly practicing both.
Controls reported no history of consistent mindfulness practice.

Since this study was conducted within a larger fMRI project, exclusion criteria for both groups were largely based on MRI safety requirements: pregnancy, claustrophobia, metal or electronic implants (e.g., pacemakers or aneurysm clips), a history of head trauma, fainting, or neurological disorders (e.g., stroke or brain tumours).

Further criteria were applied to limit confounding on neural and autonomic measures: treatment for a psychiatric disorder within the previous 12 months, use of medications or substances known to affect brain functioning, heavy alcohol consumption (more than 10 drinks per week), and heavy smoking (more than 140 cigarettes per week).

Participants were instructed to refrain from consuming caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals on the day of the testing until the laboratory session had been completed.
All sessions were conducted between 11:00 and 16:00.
Upon arrival, the participants first provided written informed consent and then completed approximately 30 minutes of computer-administered questionnaires.
This period also served as an acclimatisation phase, allowing participants to settle before physiological recording began.
Immediately after completing the baseline assessment of affect, a Polar H10 chest-strap sensor was fitted to record electrocardiographic activity throughout the acute stress protocol.
Participants first completed a five-minute seated resting baseline in a quiet room.
They were alone and instructed to keep their eyes open, remain still and not to use their phone.
The acute psychosocial stressor was a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993) adopted from Bosch et al. (2003).

text.text: The task consisted of delivering two consecutive speeches in front of two judges who maintained neutral facial expressions, refrained from interacting with participants, and took sham notes on a standardized social-performance rating scale (Fydrich et al., 1998).

text.text: Each speech was preceded by a two-minute silent preparation period and followed by four minutes of speech delivery.
All task instructions were presented automatically on a screen.
Participants remained standing in front of a camera during the entire task period, and they spoke into a microphone.
They were led to believe that their performance was being recorded for later evaluation.
If they stopped speaking before the four-minute period had elapsed, the judges instructed them to continue.
Immediately after the second speech, participants again completed the brief affect assessment and proceeded to a five-minute seated recovery period under the same conditions as at baseline.
Participants then had the chest-strap removed, and they completed the Stress and Adversity Inventory for Adults (STRAIN; Slavich & Shields, 2018).

text.text: Participants rated the extent to which each item described how they felt at the moment on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely).
Positive and negative affect subscale scores were calculated separately for each assessment by summing the relevant items.
Possible scores range from 5 to 25, with higher scores indicating greater levels of the corresponding affect.

In the original validation sample, I-PANAS-SF showed acceptable psychometric properties, including internal consistency of α = .78 for positive affect and α = .76 for negative affect (Thompson, 2007).

text.text: The sensor transmitted the data via Bluetooth to the Kubios HRV mobile application running on a smartphone.
HRV was indexed by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) between adjacent RR intervals.
RR interval recordings were preprocessed in Kubios HRV Scientific 4.2.0.

In accordance with the preregistered protocol, RMSSD was calculated for three phases: a fiveminute resting baseline, two two-minute silent anticipation periods immediately preceding the respective speeches (which were combined into a single four-minute segment representing the stress phase), and a five-minute post-stress recovery phase.
The speech periods were not included in the stress phase because vocalisation involves movement and irregular breathing that may affect HRV estimates (Druschky et al., 2020; Laborde et al., 2017).

Segments shorter than 3.5 minutes of valid recording or containing more than 5% of corrected beats were excluded.

text.text: It includes 55 stressors (26 acute events and 29 chronic difficulties; see http://www.strainsetup.com).

text.text: Participants indicated for each stressor whether they had experienced it (yes / no).
If they answered 'yes' to a specific item/stressor, they were asked follow-up questions about severity, frequency, exposure timing, and duration.

Based on participants' responses, we derived the STRAIN's two main outcome scores: (1) lifetime stressor count (i.e., objective stressor exposure) and (2) lifetime stressor severity (i.e., the perceived severity of the stressors experienced).

In addition to these totals, the STRAIN produces subscale scores related to stressor timing (early adversity occurring before age 18, adulthood, and the past year), stressor type (acute life events, chronic difficulties), 12 life domains (housing, education, work, treatment/health, marital/partner, reproduction, financial, legal/crime, other relationships, death, life-threatening situations, and possessions), and five core socialpsychological characteristics (interpersonal loss, physical danger, humiliation, entrapment, and role change/disruption).
Each subscale is available as both a count and a severity score, which results in a total of 46 subscales.

In its initial validation with community adults, the STRAIN demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability over a median interval of 13 days (rs ≥ .87 for all main indices; r = .919 for total lifetime stressor count and r = .904 for total lifetime stressor severity; Slavich & Shields, 2018); test-retest reliability was not assessed in the present sample.

text.text: To verify that the protocol elicited the intended stress response, two preliminary checks were conducted.
Paired-samples t-tests examined pre-to post-stress changes in positive and negative affect.

In parallel, the Phase-only mixed-effects model described below was used to test the omnibus effect of Phase on lnRMSSD, followed by pairwise comparisons between baseline, anticipation, and recovery phases using Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom with Tukey correction.
Next, to determine whether Group predicted poststress affect (H1), separate linear regression models were fitted for negative and positive affect (ANCOVA, as preregistered).
Each model included Group as the predictor and the corresponding pre-stress affect score, age and gender.
The latter two were included because of the age-and gender-related differences in affective reactivity (Bagley et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The latter two were included because of the age-and gender-related differences in affective reactivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bagley et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kelly et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Gender was entered as a binary indicator (female vs. not female; the five participants who selected "other" were retained in the reference category).

Group differences in phase-related changes in lnRMSSD were examined by fitting linear mixedeffects models in the HRV subsample, comprising participants with at least one valid HRV measurement across the three phases (resulting in n = 70; one participant was excluded because all three phases had more than 5% of corrected beats).
There were a total of 203 of 210 possible phase-specific observations.
Phase was treated as a within-participant factor and Group as a between-participant factor.

Age and gender were included as covariates, as previous studies have shown they have been differently associated with HRV (Adjei et al., 2018; Hamidovic et al., 2020; Hernández-Vicente et al., 2020 Koenig & Thayer, 2016), and a random intercept for participant accounted for the dependence among repeated observations.

text.text: Three nested linearmixed effects models estimated using maximum likelihood were compared: the full model (Group, Phase, Group x Phase), the no-interaction model (Group and Phase), and the no-Group model (Phase only).
First, we used the no-Group model to conduct a manipulation check to determine whether the stress protocol elicited the expected pattern of physiological stress response.
We examined the omnibus effect of Phase, followed by pairwise comparisons between the baseline, anticipation, and recovery phases, with p values adjusted for multiple comparisons with Tukey method.
Specifically, we expected lnRMSSD to decrease from baseline to anticipation and to recover thereafter.
The primary hypothesis was tested by comparing the full and no-interaction models to assess whether changes in HRV across phases differed between the groups.
The no-interaction and no-Group models were then compared to assess whether the groups differed in overall HRV levels.

Models were compared using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), with differences converted into approximate Bayes Factors to quantify the strength of evidence for competing models using the threshold of Lee and Wagenmakers (2013).
text.formatted: Models were compared using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), with differences converted into approximate Bayes Factors to quantify the strength of evidence for competing models using the threshold of <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lee and Wagenmakers (2013)</ref>.

text.text: Likelihood-ratio chi-square tests of the same nested model comparisons are reported as a frequentist robustness check.

Furthermore, meditators and controls were compared on all STRAIN subscales using independent-samples t-tests, with group differences expressed as standardised mean differences (Cohen's d) and 95% confidence intervals.

In sensitivity analyses, each primary affect and HRV model was re-estimated with each STRAIN subscale entered separately as an additional covariate (subscales were never entered jointly because they overlap, with each stressor contributing to several subscales), to establish whether the group effects on affect and HRV depended on differences in lifetime stressor exposure.
As a further robustness check, we tested 16 whether pre-to-post changes in affect differed between groups.
Because non-randomised groups may differ at baseline, baseline-adjusted and change-score estimates can diverge (Lord, 1967; Miller & Chapman, 2001).
text.formatted: Because non-randomised groups may differ at baseline, baseline-adjusted and change-score estimates can diverge <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Lord, 1967;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Miller & Chapman, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore compared pre-stress affect between groups (Welch's ttests) and fitted change-score models with the same covariates as the primary models, equivalent to testing a Group × Time interaction.

Finally, exploratory mediation analyses examined whether emotion regulation difficulties represented a potential mechanism underlying group differences in affective responses, with separate analyses for positive and negative affect.
For each outcome, an ordinary least-squares apath model examined whether groups differed in DERS scores while controlling for age and gender.
Before fitting the mixed effects models for the b and c' paths, DERS was grand-mean centered to improve interpretability of coefficients.
Affect was predicted from Group x Time, DERS, DERS x Time, and the same covariates as previous models, as well as the random intercept for participant to account for dependency.
The model was used to estimate whether DERS partially accounted for group differences in pre-stress affect and in the pre-to-post change in affect.

We additionally calculated the dissociation between these indirect effects to determine whether the indirect effect through DERS differed between pre-stress affect and the pre-to-post change in affect.
Inference was based on 95% bootstrap confidence intervals derived from 5000 participant-level resamples with replacement, with an effect supported when its interval excluded zero.

In further exploratory analyses, we examined associations between each STRAIN subscale and participants' affective and autonomic responses using partial correlations controlling for age, gender, group, and the corresponding pre-stress (baseline) value.

Lastly, within the meditator group, we examined whether practice amount was associated with the affective and autonomic outcomes, entering lifetime practice (months, square-root-transformed) and recent practice (minutes in the previous month, natural-log-transformed), each grand-mean-centred, into the corresponding models.
There were no directional hypotheses for these exploratory analyses, and these results are considered hypothesis-generating.
Missing values were not imputed.

As preregistered, each model was estimated by case-wise deletion on participants with complete data for that model, thus the analytic n varies across analyses (negative affect n = 139, positive affect n = 140, heart rate variability n = 70).

Model assumptions were evaluated through visual inspection of residual distributions and residualversus-fitted plots, of random-effect distributions for the mixed-effects models, and through influence diagnostics.
Homogeneity of regression slopes was satisfied for both analyses of covariance, and all variance inflation factors were below 1.15.

Group variances differed only for post-stress negative affect (Levene's test, p = .011), but given that groups were of similar size, analysis of covariance is robust to heterogeneity of this magnitude.
Influence diagnostics identified no case whose removal altered the significance or direction of any preregistered effect.

Exploratory associations between each STRAIN subscale and affective and autonomic responses were examined for the full sample, controlling for group, age, gender and corresponding prestress value.

Of 230 associations tested, only 10 reached p < .05, close to the 11.5 expected by chance alone (see Supplementary Figure S1 for stressor severity associations and S2 for stressor count associations).

text.text: Where associations did emerge, their direction was consistent within outcomes: greater lifetime stressor exposure was associated with lower post-stress positive affect (five associations, all negative), with higher heart rate variability during the stress phase (two associations, both work-related), with lower post-stress negative affect (two associations, both count indices), and with higher resting heart rate variability (one association).

"As a mountain of rock is unshaken by wind, so also, the wise are unperturbed by blame or by praise." -Dhammapada (Verse 81) Both classical and contemporary portrayals often depict the experienced meditator as remaining unperturbed under stress.

Buddhist scriptures use the image of a mountain "unshaken by wind" (Fronsdal, 2023), popular accounts of mindfulness promise comparable composure (Van Dam et al., 2018), and the mindfulness stress-buffering account proposes psychological and physiological pathways that may explain this phenomenon (Creswell & Lindsay, 2014; Creswell et al., 2019).

text.text: When we put these assumptions to a direct empirical test, they were supported at the psychological but not physiological level.

Specifically, long-term meditators reported lower post-stress negative affect and higher positive affect than meditation-naïve controls after accounting for pre-stress affect, consistent with the stress-buffering account.
However, their autonomic responses, measured by vagally mediated HRV, were not different from those of controls, both overall and in their trajectories across phases of the TSST (both BF01 > 14).

text.text: Longterm meditation practice was thus associated with lower negative and higher positive affect following the acute psychosocial stressor, but not with a different autonomic response to it.
These group differences were not explained by lifetime stressor exposure and were largely robust to adjustment for the various lifetime stressor domains assessed by the STRAIN.

Furthermore, differences in emotion-regulation difficulties accounted for group differences in affect before the stressor occurred but did not account for group differences in affective change following the stressor.

Our findings are consistent with the wider mindfulness-based intervention literature, in which stress buffering has also been observed more reliably for self-reported than for physiological outcomes (Morton et al., 2020) and extend that pattern to long-term meditators with more than three years of regular practice.

text.text: To our knowledge, however, only two directly comparable studies exist, and their affective findings were mixed. Rosenkranz et al. (2016) found that long-term meditators rated the TSST as less stressful than controls, whereas Gamaiunova et al. (2019) found no group differences in momentary stress ratings or post-stress negative affect, although meditators did report less shame and higher self-esteem.

text.text: These earlier studies, however, had smaller samples that could detect only large effects, and affect was assessed with either a single stressfulness rating or a post-stressor affect questionnaire alone.
The effects observed in our preregistered affect analyses were small-to-moderate (ηp² = .04-.05).
The groups also differed in affect before the stressor, and a robustness analysis of pre-to-post change showed smaller effects in the same direction that did not reach statistical significance.
Both groups showed a clear affective response to the TSST, and the advantage associated with long-term meditation therefore appears modest rather than a state of being unaffected by stressful events.
Such modest effects may nevertheless become clinically relevant if they recur across many stressors.
Consistent with this possibility, meditators reported fewer and less severe stressors over the preceding year.

Similarly, our finding of no difference in autonomic responses to the TSST between long-term meditators and controls is consistent with both prior long-term meditator studies, which found no differences in HRV (Gamaiunova et al., 2019) or salivary alpha-amylase (Rosenkranz et al., 2016).

text.text: It also aligns with meta-analytic evidence that mindfulness-based interventions do not reliably alter vagally mediated HRV (Brown et al., 2021; Christodoulou et al., 2020).

text.text: In the present study, there was a large decrease in HRV during stress anticipation and full recovery within five minutes in both groups.
Bayesian analyses provided strong to extreme evidence for the absence of group differences.
These findings suggest that any stress-buffering effects of longterm meditation may not operate through reduced autonomic reactivity to acute stress.
In fact, physiological reactivity to acute stress is a necessary human capacity that prepares the organism for challenge and maximises the chances of survival when demands are real (Sapolsky, 2004).
text.formatted: In fact, physiological reactivity to acute stress is a necessary human capacity that prepares the organism for challenge and maximises the chances of survival when demands are real <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Sapolsky, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This system is engaged by acute stressors of any kind, including the social-evaluative demands that characterise modern life and laboratory paradigms.
Blunted physiological responses to acute stress predict adverse rather than favourable outcomes (Carroll et al., 2017; Lovallo, 2011).
text.formatted: Blunted physiological responses to acute stress predict adverse rather than favourable outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Carroll et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Lovallo, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, an adaptive profile is not a damped physiological response but appropriate mobilisation followed by efficient recovery, and both groups showed this pattern.
The dissociation between affective and autonomic responding may provide clues about the processes underlying these group differences.

Subjective and physiological responses to acute stress do not necessarily covary (Campbell & Ehlert, 2012), and emotion-regulation strategies can alter subjective emotional experience more strongly than physiological responding (Webb et al., 2012; Zaehringer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Subjective and physiological responses to acute stress do not necessarily covary <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Campbell & Ehlert, 2012)</ref>, and emotion-regulation strategies can alter subjective emotional experience more strongly than physiological responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Webb et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Zaehringer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Two strategies associated with mindfulness practice are plausible candidates for the pattern observed here.

Acceptance has been linked to stress buffering in both theory and experimental research (Lindsay & Creswell, 2017; Lindsay et al., 2018), positive reappraisal has been associated with mindfulness training (Garland et al., 2011; 2015), and long-term practitioners report greater use of both strategies than controls (Gamaiunova et al., 2019).

text.text: Because strategy use was not assessed here, either during the stressor or as a disposition, these mechanisms remain to be tested directly.
The content of our affect measure provides an additional reason to consider appraisal in interpreting the present findings.
All five positive-affect items of the I-PANAS-SF assess relatively activated states.

Thus, meditators reported not only lower negative affect following the stressor, but also greater alertness, attentiveness, and determination, despite showing autonomic responses comparable to those of controls.

The combination of preserved physiological mobilisation, lower negative affect, and greater positive engagement is compatible with a more challenge-oriented rather than threat-oriented experience of evaluated performance (Seery, 2011).

text.text: A related interpretation comes from contemplative accounts of equanimity, which describe a more even-minded relationship to experience regardless of its valence (Desbordes et al., 2015; Hadash et al., 2016).

text.text: Early Buddhist texts express a similar distinction through the metaphor of the "second arrow", which separates the initial impact of an adverse event from the additional suffering generated in response to it (Bodhi, 2000).

text.text: Our findings suggest a modestly weaker second arrow in long-term meditators, although a part of the affective difference was already present before the stressor.
More broadly, any advantage associated with long-term meditation may operate across a wider timescale than the laboratory acute response captured here.
Before a stressor occurs, practice may influence how situations are selected or appraised.

Situation selection is among the earliestacting forms of emotion regulation (Gross, 2015), and differences in how avoidable stressors are managed could contribute to differences in stressor exposure over time.
text.formatted: Situation selection is among the earliestacting forms of emotion regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Gross, 2015)</ref>, and differences in how avoidable stressors are managed could contribute to differences in stressor exposure over time.

text.text: After a stressor, differences may instead emerge during recovery.

Prolonged activation sustained by processes such as rumination and worry is considered an important pathway linking acute stress to poorer health (Brosschot et al., 2005), while reductions in rumination and worry are one of the mediators of mindfulness-based interventions (Gu et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Prolonged activation sustained by processes such as rumination and worry is considered an important pathway linking acute stress to poorer health <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brosschot et al., 2005)</ref>, while reductions in rumination and worry are one of the mediators of mindfulness-based interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Gu et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility, therefore, is that group differences are more pronounced during longer-term recovery and in the periods between stressors than during the acute response itself.
Several observations in the present data are consistent with this possibility.

First, affective differences during the acute episode were smallto-moderate, while autonomic responses did not differ, suggesting that the acute response may not be where group differences are most pronounced.
Second, emotion-regulation difficulties accounted for differences in baseline affect but not for affective change following the stressor.

Although the indirect effects did not differ significantly, this pattern is consistent with emotion regulation shaping the affective context in which stress occurs more than the acute response itself.
Third, meditators reported fewer and less severe stressors over the preceding year despite no significant difference in lifetime stressor exposure.
Although exploratory, this finding raises the possibility that processes such as situation selection (Gross, 2015) or reduced stress generation (Hammen, 1991) operate over longer timescales.
text.formatted: Although exploratory, this finding raises the possibility that processes such as situation selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Gross, 2015)</ref> or reduced stress generation <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Hammen, 1991)</ref> operate over longer timescales.

text.text: Alternative explanations cannot be excluded.

For example, affect was assessed by self-report, and long-term meditators may have inferred the study hypotheses and responded in ways consistent with their identity as meditation practitioners (Grossman, 2008; Van Dam et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For example, affect was assessed by self-report, and long-term meditators may have inferred the study hypotheses and responded in ways consistent with their identity as meditation practitioners <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Grossman, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Van Dam et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: No questionnaire-based design can fully rule out this possibility.
Two observations, however, argue against a simple favourable-response account.
First, a general tendency toward favourable self-presentation would be expected to influence self-report more broadly, yet the groups did not differ in total lifetime stressor exposure.

Second, the affect measure did not ask participants directly how stressful they found the task, but instead assessed specific positive and negative affective states, making the expected direction of the study hypothesis less obvious than it would be with a direct stressfulness rating.
It is also possible that autonomic differences existed but were not captured by our measurement approach.
For instance, long-term meditators may differ in the trajectory of recovery rather than in average levels across broad phases, and such differences could be obscured by phase-averaged measures.
The present study has several strengths.
Of note, direct laboratory tests of stress reactivity in long-term meditators are rare, and the two previous studies were based on smaller samples.
We compared 80 practitioners averaging 8.4 years of practice with 68 age-and gender-matched controls, with hypotheses, measures, and primary analyses preregistered.

In addition, lifetime stressor exposure was measured directly, and group differences in affect remained robust after adjustment for nearly all STRAIN subscales, making differential stress history an unlikely explanation.

Finally, vagally mediated HRV was assessed in speech-free windows to avoid vocalisation artefacts, modelled across baseline, anticipation, and recovery rather than reduced to a difference score, and evaluated using Bayesian model comparison.
The main design limitation is inherent to research on experienced practitioners: long-term meditators are self-selected.
In principle, prospective longitudinal designs beginning before meditation practice could separate selection effects from changes associated with sustained practice.
In practice, however, such studies are difficult to conduct because only a small proportion of individuals who begin meditating are likely to sustain regular practice over many years.
Cross-sectional studies therefore remain a feasible approach for studying highly experienced meditators.
The study also had several measurement limitations.
HRV was recorded seated at baseline and recovery but standing during anticipation, and respiration was not measured.
The decline in HRV during anticipation therefore cannot be attributed solely to stressrelated vagal withdrawal.
Because the protocol was identical across groups, however, these factors are unlikely to explain the absence of group differences, and baseline and recovery remain directly comparable.
Moreover, HRV captures only one component of autonomic responding and does not provide a comprehensive measure of physiological stress responding.
Pre-session behaviours that can influence HRV, including nicotine use and physical exercise, were not restricted or recorded and may have increased measurement variability.

Finally, meditation history was self-reported and heterogeneous across traditions, limiting interpretation of dose-response effects, while the predominantly Dutch, highly educated sample constrains generalisability.
These limitations and the possibilities raised above suggest several priorities for future research.
Directly measuring challenge and threat appraisals, acceptance, and reappraisal during acute stress would allow the proposed mechanisms to be tested rather than inferred.
Laboratory studies could extend the recovery period to 30-60 minutes, repeatedly assessing affect and rumination alongside continuous HRV.

Concurrent measurement of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activity could determine whether the faster cortisol recovery previously observed in long-term meditators (Gamaiunova et al., 2019) coexists with comparable HRV responses.
text.formatted: Concurrent measurement of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activity could determine whether the faster cortisol recovery previously observed in long-term meditators <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gamaiunova et al., 2019)</ref> coexists with comparable HRV responses.

text.text: Experience-sampling studies could extend this work into daily life, tracking stress anticipation, acute response, recovery and emotion-regulation strategies as they unfold.

In conclusion, the present findings are among the first that we know of to suggest that long-term meditation practice is associated with lower negative and higher positive affect following an acute psychosocial stressor, but not with different autonomic responses to it.

At the same time, meditators reported fewer and less-severe stressors over the preceding year, suggesting that group differences may also extend beyond the acute stress response to processes operating over longer timescales.
Future research tracking stress across these different timescales will be needed to determine when, and through which processes, long-term meditators "stress less."
